source_refs.note: Answer key, Exercise 1.3 (misnumbered; errors corrected in callouts)

blocks.prompt: 1 (i) Factorize the following: \(a^{2}+4b^{2}\)
blocks.explanation: This is a sum of two squares. With real numbers it cannot be factorized, but with complex numbers it can, because \(i^{2}=-1\) turns a plus into a minus. Plan: write both terms as squares, change the sum into a difference of squares, then use \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\).
steps:
Step 1: Write both terms as squares
\[4b^{2}=(2b)^{2}\]
\[a^{2}+4b^{2}=a^{2}+(2b)^{2}\]
Why: The difference-of-squares rule needs each term in the form (something)\(^{2}\).

Step 2: Change the plus into a minus with i
\[(2bi)^{2}=4b^{2}i^{2}=-4b^{2}\]
\[a^{2}+(2b)^{2}=a^{2}-(2bi)^{2}\]
Why: Since \(i^{2}=-1\), subtracting \((2bi)^{2}\) is the same as adding \(4b^{2}\). Now we have a difference of squares.

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[a^{2}-(2bi)^{2}\]
\[=(a+2bi)(a-2bi)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=a\), \(B=2bi\).

Check: multiply the factors back
\[(a+2bi)(a-2bi)\]
\[=a^{2}-4b^{2}i^{2}\]
\[=a^{2}+4b^{2}\]
Why: We get the original expression, so the factorization is correct.

blocks.prompt: 1 (ii) Factorize the following: \(9a^{2}+16b^{2}\)
blocks.explanation: Again a sum of two squares: \(9a^{2}=(3a)^{2}\) and \(16b^{2}=(4b)^{2}\). Plan: turn \(+(4b)^{2}\) into \(-(4bi)^{2}\) and use the difference of squares.
steps:
Step 1: Write both terms as squares
\[9a^{2}=(3a)^{2}\]
\[16b^{2}=(4b)^{2}\]
Why: \(3^{2}=9\) and \(4^{2}=16\), so each term is a perfect square.

Step 2: Change the plus into a minus
\[(4bi)^{2}=16b^{2}i^{2}=-16b^{2}\]
\[9a^{2}+16b^{2}=(3a)^{2}-(4bi)^{2}\]
Why: Because \(i^{2}=-1\), minus \((4bi)^{2}\) equals plus \(16b^{2}\).

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[(3a)^{2}-(4bi)^{2}\]
\[=(3a+4bi)(3a-4bi)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=3a\), \(B=4bi\).

Check: multiply back
\[(3a+4bi)(3a-4bi)\]
\[=9a^{2}-16b^{2}i^{2}\]
\[=9a^{2}+16b^{2}\]
Why: The product is the given expression.

blocks.prompt: 1 (iii) Factorize the following: \(3x^{2}+3y^{2}\)
blocks.explanation: Both terms have the common factor 3. Take it out first; what is left, \(x^{2}+y^{2}\), is a sum of squares, which we factorize with \(i\).
steps:
Step 1: Take out the common factor 3
\[3x^{2}+3y^{2}=3(x^{2}+y^{2})\]
Why: Always take out a common factor first; it makes the bracket simpler.

Step 2: Change the sum into a difference
\[(iy)^{2}=i^{2}y^{2}=-y^{2}\]
\[x^{2}+y^{2}=x^{2}-(iy)^{2}\]
Why: Using \(i^{2}=-1\), \(+y^{2}\) is the same as \(-(iy)^{2}\).

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[3\left(x^{2}-(iy)^{2}\right)\]
\[=3(x+iy)(x-iy)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=x\), \(B=iy\); the 3 stays in front.

Check: multiply back
\[3(x+iy)(x-iy)\]
\[=3(x^{2}-i^{2}y^{2})\]
\[=3x^{2}+3y^{2}\]
Why: We get the given expression.

blocks.prompt: 1 (iv) Factorize the following: \(144x^{2}+225y^{2}\)
blocks.explanation: The numbers 144 and 225 share the factor 9 (\(144=9\times16\), \(225=9\times25\)). Take out 9, write the rest as a sum of squares, and factorize it with \(i\).
steps:
Step 1: Take out the common factor 9
\[144x^{2}+225y^{2}\]
\[=9(16x^{2}+25y^{2})\]
Why: 9 is the highest common factor of 144 and 225, so the bracket becomes as small as possible.

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[9\left((4x)^{2}-(5yi)^{2}\right)\]
\[=9(4x+5yi)(4x-5yi)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=4x\), \(B=5yi\).

Check: multiply back
\[9(16x^{2}-25y^{2}i^{2})\]
\[=9(16x^{2}+25y^{2})\]
\[=144x^{2}+225y^{2}\]
Why: The product is the given expression. (The answer key writes the same factors as \(9(4x+i5y)(4x-i5y)\).)

blocks.prompt: 1 (v) Factorize the following: \(z^{2}-2iz-1\)
blocks.explanation: A quadratic in \(z\). Compare it with the perfect square \((z-k)^{2}=z^{2}-2kz+k^{2}\): the middle term \(-2iz\) suggests \(k=i\). Plan: complete the square and see whether anything is left over.
steps:
Step 1: Halve the coefficient of z and square it
\[\dfrac{-2i}{2}=-i\]
\[(-i)^{2}=i^{2}=-1\]
Why: In completing the square we always add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\).

Step 2: Notice the constant is already that square
\[z^{2}-2iz-1\]
\[=z^{2}-2iz+(-i)^{2}\]
\[=(z-i)^{2}\]
Why: The constant term \(-1\) is exactly \((-i)^{2}\), so the whole expression is a perfect square with nothing left over.

Check: multiply back
\[(z-i)(z-i)\]
\[=z^{2}-iz-iz+i^{2}\]
\[=z^{2}-2iz-1\]
Why: We get the given expression. The two linear factors are equal (the root \(z=i\) is repeated).

blocks.prompt: 1 (vi) Factorize the following: \(z^{2}+6z+13\)
blocks.explanation: A quadratic in \(z\) with no real factors (\(b^{2}-4ac=36-52<0\)). Plan: complete the square, write the leftover positive number as \(-(\ldots i)^{2}\), then use the difference of squares.
steps:
Step 2: Write +4 as minus a square
\[(2i)^{2}=4i^{2}=-4\]
\[(z+3)^{2}+4=(z+3)^{2}-(2i)^{2}\]
Why: Since \((2i)^{2}=-4\), adding 4 is the same as subtracting \((2i)^{2}\).

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[(z+3)^{2}-(2i)^{2}\]
\[=(z+3+2i)(z+3-2i)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=z+3\), \(B=2i\).

Check: multiply back
\[(z+3)^{2}-(2i)^{2}\]
\[=z^{2}+6z+9+4\]
\[=z^{2}+6z+13\]
Why: The product is the given expression.

blocks.prompt: 1 (vii) Factorize the following: \(z^{2}+4z+5\)
blocks.explanation: Same type as (vi). Complete the square, write the leftover \(+1\) as \(-i^{2}\), then use the difference of squares.
steps:
Step 1: Complete the square
\[\left(\dfrac{4}{2}\right)^{2}=4\]
\[z^{2}+4z+5=(z^{2}+4z+4)+1\]
\[=(z+2)^{2}+1\]
Why: Half of 4 is 2 and \(2^{2}=4\), so we split 5 as \(4+1\).

Step 3: Use the difference of squares
\[(z+2)^{2}-i^{2}\]
\[=(z+2+i)(z+2-i)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=z+2\), \(B=i\).

Check: multiply back
\[(z+2)^{2}-i^{2}\]
\[=z^{2}+4z+4+1\]
\[=z^{2}+4z+5\]
Why: The product is the given expression.

blocks.prompt: 1 (viii) [printed as (vii)] Factorize the following: \(2z^{2}-22z+65\)
blocks.explanation: A quadratic whose leading coefficient is 2. Take the 2 out first so the \(z^{2}\) coefficient is 1, complete the square inside, and keep the 2 in front of the final answer.
steps:
Step 1: Take out the leading coefficient 2
\[2z^{2}-22z+65\]
\[=2\left(z^{2}-11z+\dfrac{65}{2}\right)\]
Why: Completing the square is easiest when the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) is 1.

Step 2: Complete the square inside
\[\left(\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{121}{4}\]
\[\dfrac{65}{2}=\dfrac{130}{4}=\dfrac{121}{4}+\dfrac{9}{4}\]
\[z^{2}-11z+\dfrac{65}{2}\]
\[=\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^{2}+\dfrac{9}{4}\]
Why: Half of \(-11\) is \(-\frac{11}{2}\); its square \(\frac{121}{4}\) completes the square, and \(\frac{9}{4}\) is left over.

Step 3: Write the leftover as minus a square
\[\left(\dfrac{3i}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{9i^{2}}{4}=-\dfrac{9}{4}\]
\[\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^{2}-\left(\dfrac{3i}{2}\right)^{2}\]
Why: So \(+\frac{9}{4}=-\left(\frac{3i}{2}\right)^{2}\), which gives a difference of squares.

Step 4: Factorize and put the 2 back
\[\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}+\dfrac{3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}-\dfrac{3i}{2}\right)\]
\[=\left(z-\dfrac{11-3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\dfrac{11+3i}{2}\right)\]
\[2z^{2}-22z+65\]
\[=2\left(z-\dfrac{11-3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\dfrac{11+3i}{2}\right)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). The 2 taken out in Step 1 must stay in front, otherwise the product is only half of the given polynomial.

Check: multiply back
\[\left(z-\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^{2}+\dfrac{9}{4}\]
\[=z^{2}-11z+\dfrac{130}{4}\]
\[2\left(z^{2}-11z+\dfrac{65}{2}\right)=2z^{2}-22z+65\]
Why: Multiplying by 2 gives back the given polynomial.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book labels this part (vii) a second time; here it is part (viii). The answer key (page 297) prints \(\left(z-\frac{11-3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\frac{11+3i}{2}\right)\) without the leading factor 2. That product expands to \(z^{2}-11z+\frac{65}{2}\), only half of the given polynomial. Correct: \(2z^{2}-22z+65=2\left(z-\frac{11-3i}{2}\right)\left(z-\frac{11+3i}{2}\right)\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (i) Factorize the following polynomial into its linear factors: \(z^{3}+8\)
blocks.explanation: A cubic has exactly three linear factors over the complex numbers. \(z^{3}+8=z^{3}+2^{3}\) is a sum of cubes: that gives one linear factor and a quadratic; then factorize the quadratic by completing the square.
steps:
Step 2: Complete the square in the quadratic
\[z^{2}-2z+4=(z^{2}-2z+1)+3\]
\[=(z-1)^{2}+3\]
Why: Half of \(-2\) is \(-1\) and \((-1)^{2}=1\), so split 4 as \(1+3\). (Its discriminant \(4-16<0\), so it has no real factors.)

Step 3: Write +3 as minus a square and factorize
\[(i\sqrt{3})^{2}=3i^{2}=-3\]
\[(z-1)^{2}-(i\sqrt{3})^{2}\]
\[=(z-1-i\sqrt{3})(z-1+i\sqrt{3})\]
\[=\left(z-(1+i\sqrt{3})\right)\left(z-(1-i\sqrt{3})\right)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=z-1\), \(B=i\sqrt{3}\).

Check: one complex root
\[(1+i\sqrt{3})^{2}=-2+2i\sqrt{3}\]
\[(1+i\sqrt{3})^{3}=(-2+2i\sqrt{3})(1+i\sqrt{3})\]
\[=-2-6=-8\]
Why: So \(z=1+i\sqrt{3}\) makes \(z^{3}+8=0\): the factor is correct.

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) Factorize the following polynomial into its linear factors: \(z^{3}+27\)
blocks.explanation: Same method as (i): \(27=3^{3}\), so use the sum of cubes, then factorize the quadratic factor by completing the square.
steps:
Step 2: Complete the square
\[\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{9}{4}\]
\[9=\dfrac{9}{4}+\dfrac{27}{4}\]
\[z^{2}-3z+9=\left(z-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{2}+\dfrac{27}{4}\]
Why: Half of \(-3\) is \(-\frac{3}{2}\); its square is \(\frac{9}{4}\), and \(9-\frac{9}{4}=\frac{27}{4}\) is left over.

Step 3: Write the leftover as minus a square
\[\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{27i^{2}}{4}=-\dfrac{27}{4}\]
Why: \((3\sqrt{3})^{2}=9\times3=27\), so \(+\frac{27}{4}=-\left(\frac{3\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\right)^{2}\).

Step 4: Use the difference of squares
\[\left(z-\dfrac{3}{2}-\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\right)\]
\[\times\left(z-\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\right)\]
\[=\left(z-\dfrac{3+3\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\right)\left(z-\dfrac{3-3\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\right)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=z-\frac{3}{2}\), \(B=\frac{3\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\).

Check: sum and product of the two complex roots
\[\dfrac{3+3\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}+\dfrac{3-3\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}=3\]
\[\dfrac{9+27}{4}=9\]
Why: A quadratic \(z^{2}-3z+9\) must have roots with sum 3 and product 9, and these do.

blocks.prompt: 2 (iii) [printed as (ii)] Factorize the following polynomial into its linear factors: \(z^{3}-2z^{2}+16z-32\)
blocks.explanation: Four terms: try grouping in pairs. If both pairs give the same bracket, take it out; the remaining sum of squares is split with \(i\).
steps:
Step 1: Group in pairs
\[z^{2}(z-2)+16(z-2)\]
\[=(z-2)(z^{2}+16)\]
Why: \(z^{2}\) is common to the first pair and 16 to the second; both leave \((z-2)\).

Step 2: Factorize the sum of squares
\[z^{2}+16=z^{2}-(4i)^{2}\]
\[=(z-4i)(z+4i)\]
Why: \((4i)^{2}=-16\), so \(+16=-(4i)^{2}\); then the difference of squares.

blocks.prompt: 2 (iv) [printed as (iii)] Factorize the following polynomial into its linear factors: \(z^{4}+21z^{2}-100\)
blocks.explanation: Only \(z^{4}\), \(z^{2}\) and a constant appear, so it is a quadratic in \(z^{2}\). Put \(u=z^{2}\), factorize, then split each bracket into linear factors (four in all).
steps:
Step 1: Treat it as a quadratic in z²
\[u=z^{2}:\ u^{2}+21u-100\]
\[=(u+25)(u-4)\]
Why: We need two numbers with product \(-100\) and sum 21: \(25\) and \(-4\).

Step 3: Split each bracket
\[z^{2}+25=z^{2}-(5i)^{2}\]
\[=(z+5i)(z-5i)\]
\[z^{2}-4=(z+2)(z-2)\]
Why: \(+25=-(5i)^{2}\); \(z^{2}-4\) is an ordinary difference of squares.

Check: constant and middle terms
\[25\times(-4)=-100\]
\[25+(-4)=21\]
Why: These match \(-100\) and \(21z^{2}\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (v) [printed as (iv)] Factorize the following polynomial into its linear factors: \(z^{4}-16\)
blocks.explanation: \(z^{4}=(z^{2})^{2}\) and \(16=4^{2}\): a difference of squares. Use it once, then split each bracket again.
steps:
Step 1: Difference of squares
\[z^{4}-16=(z^{2})^{2}-4^{2}\]
\[=(z^{2}-4)(z^{2}+4)\]
Why: Difference of squares: \(A^{2}-B^{2}=(A+B)(A-B)\). Here \(A=z^{2}\), \(B=4\).

Check: put z = 2i
\[(2i)^{4}=16i^{4}=16\]
\[16-16=0\]
Why: So \(2i\) is a root, as the factor \((z-2i)\) says.

blocks.prompt: 2 (vi) [printed as (iii)] Factorize the following polynomial into its linear factors: \(z^{4}+3z^{2}-4\)
blocks.explanation: Only \(z^{4}\), \(z^{2}\) and a constant appear, so it is a quadratic in \(z^{2}\). Put \(u=z^{2}\), factorize, then split each bracket into linear factors (four in all).
steps:
Step 1: Factorize as a quadratic in z²
\[z^{4}+3z^{2}-4=(z^{2}+4)(z^{2}-1)\]
Why: Two numbers with product \(-4\) and sum 3: \(4\) and \(-1\).

Step 2: Split each bracket
\[z^{2}+4=(z+2i)(z-2i)\]
\[z^{2}-1=(z+1)(z-1)\]
Why: \(+4=-(2i)^{2}\); \(z^{2}-1\) is a difference of squares.

Check: constant and middle terms
\[4\times(-1)=-4\]
\[4+(-1)=3\]
Why: These match \(-4\) and \(3z^{2}\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (vii) [printed as (iv)] Factorize the following polynomial into its linear factors: \(z^{4}+5z^{2}+6\)
blocks.explanation: Only \(z^{4}\), \(z^{2}\) and a constant appear, so it is a quadratic in \(z^{2}\). Put \(u=z^{2}\), factorize, then split each bracket into linear factors (four in all). Here both brackets will be sums, so both need \(i\).
steps:
Step 1: Factorize as a quadratic in z²
\[z^{4}+5z^{2}+6=(z^{2}+2)(z^{2}+3)\]
Why: Two numbers with product 6 and sum 5: 2 and 3.

Step 2: Write each plus as minus a square
\[(\sqrt{2}\,i)^{2}=-2,\ (\sqrt{3}\,i)^{2}=-3\]
\[z^{2}+2=(z+\sqrt{2}\,i)(z-\sqrt{2}\,i)\]
\[z^{2}+3=(z+\sqrt{3}\,i)(z-\sqrt{3}\,i)\]
Why: 2 and 3 are not perfect squares, so we use \(\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{3}\); \(i\) supplies the minus sign.

Check: constant and middle terms
\[2\times3=6\]
\[2+3=5\]
Why: These match \(+6\) and \(5z^{2}\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (viii) [printed as (v)] Factorize the following polynomial into its linear factors: \(z^{4}+7z^{2}-144\)
blocks.explanation: Only \(z^{4}\), \(z^{2}\) and a constant appear, so it is a quadratic in \(z^{2}\). Put \(u=z^{2}\), factorize, then split each bracket into linear factors (four in all).
steps:
Step 1: Factorize as a quadratic in z²
\[z^{4}+7z^{2}-144=(z^{2}+16)(z^{2}-9)\]
Why: Two numbers with product \(-144\) and sum 7: 16 and \(-9\).

Step 2: Split each bracket
\[z^{2}+16=(z+4i)(z-4i)\]
\[z^{2}-9=(z+3)(z-3)\]
Why: \(+16=-(4i)^{2}\); \(z^{2}-9\) is a difference of squares.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the eight part labels of this question as (i), (ii), (ii), (iii), (iv), (iii), (iv), (v); here they are numbered (i) to (viii). The answer key (page 297) gives only six answers, labelled (i) to (vi): its (iii), (iv), (v) and (vi) are the answers to parts (iii), (v), (vi) and (vii) here, and it gives no answer for part (iv) or part (viii). The missing answers are \(z^{4}+21z^{2}-100=(z+2)(z-2)(z+5i)(z-5i)\) and \(z^{4}+7z^{2}-144=(z+3)(z-3)(z+4i)(z-4i)\).

blocks.prompt: 3 Find the roots of \(z^{4}+7z^{2}-144=0\) and hence express it as a product of linear factors.
blocks.explanation: First find the four roots (degree 4 means four roots). Put \(u=z^{2}\) to get a quadratic in \(u\), solve it, then take square roots. Each root \(r\) gives a linear factor \((z-r)\) by the corollary of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.
steps:
Step 1: Change to a quadratic in u
\[u=z^{2}\]
\[u^{2}+7u-144=0\]
Why: \(z^{4}=(z^{2})^{2}=u^{2}\), so the equation becomes an ordinary quadratic.

Step 2: Solve for u
\[u=\dfrac{-7\pm\sqrt{49+576}}{2}\]
\[=\dfrac{-7\pm25}{2}\]
\[u=9\ \text{or}\ u=-16\]
Why: Quadratic formula with \(a=1\), \(b=7\), \(c=-144\); \(\sqrt{625}=25\). (Factorizing \((u-9)(u+16)\) gives the same.)

Step 3: Go back to z
\[z^{2}=9\Rightarrow z=\pm3\]
\[z^{2}=-16\Rightarrow z=\pm\sqrt{-16}=\pm4i\]
Why: Taking a square root always gives two values, \(\pm\); and \(\sqrt{-16}=\sqrt{16}\,\sqrt{-1}=4i\).

Step 4: Write the linear factors
\[z^{4}+7z^{2}-144\]
\[=(z-3)(z+3)(z-4i)(z+4i)\]
Why: The coefficient of \(z^{4}\) is 1, so \(P(z)=1\cdot(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})(z-z_{3})(z-z_{4})\).

blocks.prompt: 4 (i) Solve the following complex quadratic equation by completing square method: \(2z^{2}-3z+4=0\)
blocks.explanation: Completing the square: make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1, move the constant to the right, add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\) to both sides, then take square roots (the right side is negative, so the roots are complex).
steps:
Step 1: Divide by 2 and move the constant
\[z^{2}-\dfrac{3}{2}z+2=0\]
\[z^{2}-\dfrac{3}{2}z=-2\]
Why: Completing the square needs the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) to be 1.

Step 2: Add (3/4)² to both sides
\[\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{9}{16}\]
\[\left(z-\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{2}=-2+\dfrac{9}{16}\]
\[=-\dfrac{23}{16}\]
Why: Adding the same number to both sides keeps the equation true and makes the left side a perfect square.

Step 3: Take square roots
\[z-\dfrac{3}{4}=\pm\sqrt{-\dfrac{23}{16}}=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{23}}{4}\,i\]
\[z=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{23}\,i}{4}\]
Why: \(\sqrt{-k}=i\sqrt{k}\) for \(k>0\); remember \(\pm\).

Check: sum and product
\[\text{sum}=\dfrac{6}{4}=\dfrac{3}{2}=-\dfrac{b}{a}\]
\[\text{product}=\dfrac{9+23}{16}=2=\dfrac{c}{a}\]
Why: For \(az^{2}+bz+c=0\) the roots must have sum \(-b/a\) and product \(c/a\). Here \(-b/a=3/2\), \(c/a=4/2=2\).

blocks.prompt: 4 (ii) Solve the following complex quadratic equation by completing square method: \(z^{2}-6z+30=0\)
blocks.explanation: Completing the square: make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1, move the constant to the right, add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\) to both sides, then take square roots (the right side is negative, so the roots are complex).
steps:
Step 1: Move the constant
\[z^{2}-6z=-30\]
Why: The coefficient of \(z^{2}\) is already 1.

Step 3: Take square roots
\[z-3=\pm\sqrt{-21}=\pm i\sqrt{21}\]
\[z=3\pm i\sqrt{21}\]
Why: \(\sqrt{-21}=i\sqrt{21}\); then add 3 to both sides.

Check: sum and product
\[\text{sum}=6=-\dfrac{b}{a}\]
\[\text{product}=9+21=30=\dfrac{c}{a}\]
Why: For \(az^{2}+bz+c=0\) the roots must have sum \(-b/a\) and product \(c/a\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (page 297) prints \(z=2\pm i\sqrt{21}\). This is wrong: the real part is half of 6, i.e. 3 (with real part 2 the roots would add up to 4, not 6). Correct: \(z=3\pm i\sqrt{21}\).

blocks.prompt: 4 (iii) Solve the following complex quadratic equation by completing square method: \(3z^{2}-18z+50=0\)
blocks.explanation: Completing the square: make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1, move the constant to the right, add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\) to both sides, then take square roots (the right side is negative, so the roots are complex).
steps:
Step 1: Divide by 3 and move the constant
\[z^{2}-6z+\dfrac{50}{3}=0\]
\[z^{2}-6z=-\dfrac{50}{3}\]
Why: Make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1.

Step 2: Add 3² = 9 to both sides
\[(z-3)^{2}=9-\dfrac{50}{3}\]
\[=\dfrac{27-50}{3}=-\dfrac{23}{3}\]
Why: Half of \(-6\) is \(-3\); write 9 as \(\frac{27}{3}\) to subtract.

Step 3: Take square roots
\[z-3=\pm i\sqrt{\dfrac{23}{3}}\]
\[\sqrt{\dfrac{23}{3}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{69}}{3}\]
\[z=3\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{69}}{3}\,i\]
Why: Rationalize: \(\sqrt{\frac{23}{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{23}\sqrt{3}}{3}=\frac{\sqrt{69}}{3}\).

Check: sum and product
\[\text{sum}=6=\dfrac{18}{3}\]
\[\text{product}=9+\dfrac{69}{9}=\dfrac{50}{3}\]
Why: For \(az^{2}+bz+c=0\) the roots must have sum \(-b/a\) and product \(c/a\). Here \(-b/a=18/3=6\), \(c/a=50/3\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (page 297) prints \(z=3\pm i\). This is wrong: \(z=3+i\) gives \(3(3+i)^{2}-18(3+i)+50=20\), not 0. Completing the square gives \((z-3)^{2}=-\frac{23}{3}\). Correct: \(z=3\pm\frac{\sqrt{69}}{3}\,i\).

blocks.prompt: 4 (iv) [printed as (i)] Solve the following complex quadratic equation by completing square method: \(z^{2}+4z+13=0\)
blocks.explanation: Completing the square: make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1, move the constant to the right, add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\) to both sides, then take square roots (the right side is negative, so the roots are complex).
steps:
Step 1: Move the constant
\[z^{2}+4z=-13\]
Why: The coefficient of \(z^{2}\) is already 1.

Step 2: Add 2² = 4 to both sides
\[z^{2}+4z+4=-13+4\]
\[(z+2)^{2}=-9\]
Why: Half of 4 is 2 and \(2^{2}=4\).

Step 3: Take square roots
\[z+2=\pm\sqrt{-9}=\pm3i\]
\[z=-2\pm3i\]
Why: \(\sqrt{-9}=3i\); subtract 2 from both sides.

Check: sum and product
\[\text{sum}=-4=-\dfrac{b}{a}\]
\[\text{product}=4+9=13=\dfrac{c}{a}\]
Why: For \(az^{2}+bz+c=0\) the roots must have sum \(-b/a\) and product \(c/a\).

blocks.prompt: 4 (v) [printed as (ii)] Solve the following complex quadratic equation by completing square method: \(2z^{2}+6z+9=0\)
blocks.explanation: Completing the square: make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1, move the constant to the right, add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\) to both sides, then take square roots (the right side is negative, so the roots are complex).
steps:
Step 1: Divide by 2 and move the constant
\[z^{2}+3z+\dfrac{9}{2}=0\]
\[z^{2}+3z=-\dfrac{9}{2}\]
Why: Make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1.

Step 2: Add (3/2)² to both sides
\[\left(z+\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{2}=-\dfrac{9}{2}+\dfrac{9}{4}\]
\[=-\dfrac{9}{4}\]
Why: Half of 3 is \(\frac{3}{2}\) and \(\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{9}{4}\).

Step 3: Take square roots
\[z+\dfrac{3}{2}=\pm\dfrac{3}{2}\,i\]
\[z=-\dfrac{3}{2}\pm\dfrac{3}{2}\,i\]
Why: \(\sqrt{-\frac{9}{4}}=\frac{3}{2}i\).

Check: sum and product
\[\text{sum}=-3=-\dfrac{6}{2}\]
\[\text{product}=\dfrac{9}{4}+\dfrac{9}{4}=\dfrac{9}{2}\]
Why: For \(az^{2}+bz+c=0\) the roots must have sum \(-b/a\) and product \(c/a\).

blocks.prompt: 4 (vi) [printed as (iii)] Solve the following complex quadratic equation by completing square method: \(3z^{2}-5z+7=0\)
blocks.explanation: Completing the square: make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1, move the constant to the right, add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\) to both sides, then take square roots (the right side is negative, so the roots are complex).
steps:
Step 1: Divide by 3 and move the constant
\[z^{2}-\dfrac{5}{3}z+\dfrac{7}{3}=0\]
\[z^{2}-\dfrac{5}{3}z=-\dfrac{7}{3}\]
Why: Make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1.

Step 2: Add (5/6)² to both sides
\[\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{25}{36}\]
\[\left(z-\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{2}=-\dfrac{7}{3}+\dfrac{25}{36}\]
\[=\dfrac{-84+25}{36}=-\dfrac{59}{36}\]
Why: Common denominator 36: \(\frac{7}{3}=\frac{84}{36}\).

Step 3: Take square roots
\[z-\dfrac{5}{6}=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{59}}{6}\,i\]
\[z=\dfrac{5\pm i\sqrt{59}}{6}\]
Why: \(\sqrt{-\frac{59}{36}}=\frac{\sqrt{59}}{6}i\) since \(\sqrt{36}=6\).

Check: sum and product
\[\text{sum}=\dfrac{10}{6}=\dfrac{5}{3}\]
\[\text{product}=\dfrac{25+59}{36}=\dfrac{7}{3}\]
Why: For \(az^{2}+bz+c=0\) the roots must have sum \(-b/a\) and product \(c/a\). Here \(-b/a=5/3\), \(c/a=7/3\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book labels the six parts of this question (i), (ii), (iii), (i), (ii), (iii); here they are (i) to (vi). For this part the answer key (page 297) prints \(z=\frac{5\pm i\sqrt{41}}{6}\). This is wrong: the discriminant is \(25-84=-59\), not \(-41\). Correct: \(z=\frac{5\pm i\sqrt{59}}{6}\).

blocks.prompt: 5 (i) Solve the following equations: \(2z^{4}-32=0\)
blocks.explanation: Degree 4, so expect four roots. Take out the common factor 2, then factorize \(z^{4}-16\) completely and set each factor equal to zero.
steps:
Step 1: Take out the common factor 2
\[2(z^{4}-16)=0\]
\[z^{4}-16=0\]
Why: 2 is not zero, so the bracket must be zero.

Step 2: Factorize completely
\[(z^{2}-4)(z^{2}+4)=0\]
\[(z-2)(z+2)(z-2i)(z+2i)=0\]
Why: Difference of squares twice; \(+4=-(2i)^{2}\).

Step 3: Set each factor equal to zero
\[z=2,\ -2,\ 2i,\ -2i\]
Why: A product is zero only if one of its factors is zero.

blocks.prompt: 5 (ii) Solve the following equations: \(3z^{5}-243z=0\)
blocks.explanation: Degree 5, so five roots. Take out the common factor \(3z\) (do not divide by \(z\), or the root 0 is lost), then factorize \(z^{4}-81\).
steps:
Step 2: Factorize z⁴ − 81
\[z^{4}-81=(z^{2}-9)(z^{2}+9)\]
\[=(z-3)(z+3)(z-3i)(z+3i)\]
Why: Difference of squares twice; \(+9=-(3i)^{2}\).

Step 3: Set each factor equal to zero
\[3z(z-3)(z+3)(z-3i)(z+3i)=0\]
\[z=0,\ 3,\ -3,\ 3i,\ -3i\]
Why: \(3z=0\) gives \(z=0\); the other four factors give the rest.

blocks.prompt: 5 (iii) Solve the following equations: \(5z^{5}-5z=0\)
blocks.explanation: Five roots expected. Take out \(5z\), then factorize \(z^{4}-1\) completely.
steps:
Step 1: Take out 5z
\[5z(z^{4}-1)=0\]
Why: Both terms contain 5 and \(z\).

Step 2: Factorize z⁴ − 1
\[z^{4}-1=(z^{2}-1)(z^{2}+1)\]
\[=(z-1)(z+1)(z-i)(z+i)\]
Why: Difference of squares twice; \(+1=-i^{2}\).

Step 3: Set each factor equal to zero
\[z=0,\ 1,\ -1,\ i,\ -i\]
Why: One root from \(5z\) and four from the brackets.

blocks.prompt: 5 (iv) Solve the following equations: \(z^{3}-5z^{2}+z-5=0\)
blocks.explanation: A cubic with four terms: group in pairs to find a common bracket, then factorize the sum of squares that remains.
steps:
Step 1: Group in pairs
\[z^{2}(z-5)+1(z-5)=0\]
\[(z-5)(z^{2}+1)=0\]
Why: Both pairs contain \((z-5)\).

Step 3: Set each factor equal to zero
\[z=5,\ i,\ -i\]
Why: Three factors, three roots.

Check: put z = 5
\[125-125+5-5=0\]
Why: \(z=5\) satisfies the equation.

blocks.prompt: 5 (v) Solve the following equations: \(4z^{4}-25z^{2}+21=0\)
blocks.explanation: Only \(z^{4}\), \(z^{2}\) and a constant: a quadratic in \(z^{2}\). Put \(u=z^{2}\), solve for \(u\), then take square roots (here all four roots turn out real).
steps:
Step 2: Factorize by splitting the middle term
\[4u^{2}-21u-4u+21=0\]
\[u(4u-21)-1(4u-21)=0\]
\[(4u-21)(u-1)=0\]
Why: \(4\times21=84\); the numbers with product 84 and sum \(-25\) are \(-21\) and \(-4\).

Step 3: Solve for u, then for z
\[u=\dfrac{21}{4}\Rightarrow z=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{2}\]
\[u=1\Rightarrow z=\pm1\]
Why: \(\sqrt{\frac{21}{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{21}}{2}\); keep both signs.

Check: put z = 1
\[4-25+21=0\]
Why: \(z=1\) satisfies the equation.

blocks.prompt: 5 (vi) Solve the following equations: \(z^{3}+z^{2}+z+1=0\)
blocks.explanation: Four terms: group in pairs, take out the common bracket, then factorize \(z^{2}+1\).
steps:
Step 1: Group in pairs
\[z^{2}(z+1)+1(z+1)=0\]
\[(z+1)(z^{2}+1)=0\]
Why: Both pairs contain \((z+1)\).

Step 3: Set each factor equal to zero
\[z=-1,\ i,\ -i\]
Why: Each factor gives one root.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (page 297) prints no answers for Question 5. The three answers it prints under the labels 5, 6 and 7 belong to Questions 6, 7 and 8.

blocks.prompt: 6 Find a polynomial of degree 3 with zeros \(3,\ -2i,\ 2i\) and satisfying \(P(1)=20\).
blocks.explanation: We build a polynomial from its zeros: each zero \(r\) gives a factor \((z-r)\), and \(P(z)=a(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots\) with an unknown number \(a\) in front. The extra condition fixes \(a\). Then expand and check.
steps:
Step 1: Write the factors
\[P(z)=a(z-3)(z+2i)(z-2i)\]
Why: Zero 3 gives \((z-3)\); zero \(-2i\) gives \((z+2i)\); zero \(2i\) gives \((z-2i)\). Three factors for degree 3.

Step 2: Multiply the conjugate pair
\[(z+2i)(z-2i)=z^{2}-4i^{2}=z^{2}+4\]
\[P(z)=a(z-3)(z^{2}+4)\]
Why: A conjugate pair always multiplies to a real quadratic; \(i\) disappears.

Step 4: Expand
\[(z-3)(z^{2}+4)=z^{3}-3z^{2}+4z-12\]
\[P(z)=-2z^{3}+6z^{2}-8z+24\]
Why: Multiply every term by \(-2\); each sign flips.

Check: P(1) and P(3)
\[P(1)=-2+6-8+24=20\]
\[P(3)=-54+54-24+24=0\]
Why: The condition holds and 3 is a zero.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (page 297) prints this answer under the label 5, as \(x=-2z^{3}+6z^{2}-8z+24\). It is the answer to Question 6, and it should read \(P(z)=\) rather than \(x=\). The polynomial itself is correct.

blocks.prompt: 7 Find a polynomial of degree 4 with zeros \(2i,\ -2i,\ 1,\ -1\), and satisfying \(P(2)=240\).
blocks.explanation: We build a polynomial from its zeros: each zero \(r\) gives a factor \((z-r)\), and \(P(z)=a(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots\) with an unknown number \(a\) in front. The extra condition fixes \(a\). Then expand and check.
steps:
Step 1: Write the factors and pair them
\[P(z)=a(z-2i)(z+2i)(z-1)(z+1)\]
\[=a(z^{2}+4)(z^{2}-1)\]
Why: Each pair is a difference of squares: \((z-2i)(z+2i)=z^{2}+4\), \((z-1)(z+1)=z^{2}-1\).

Check: P(2)
\[10(16)+30(4)-40=240\]
Why: The condition holds.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (page 297) prints this answer under the label 6, as \(x=10z^{4}+30z^{2}-40\). It is the answer to Question 7, and it should read \(P(z)=\) rather than \(x=\). The polynomial itself is correct.

blocks.prompt: 8 Find a polynomial of degree 4 with zeros \(4,\ -4,\ 1+i,\ 1-i\) and satisfying \(P(2)=72\).
blocks.explanation: We build a polynomial from its zeros: each zero \(r\) gives a factor \((z-r)\), and \(P(z)=a(z-z_{1})(z-z_{2})\cdots\) with an unknown number \(a\) in front. The extra condition fixes \(a\). Then expand and check. Here \(1+i\) and \(1-i\) are a conjugate pair.
steps:
Step 1: Multiply the real pair
\[(z-4)(z+4)=z^{2}-16\]
Why: Difference of squares.

Step 2: Multiply the conjugate pair
\[(z-1-i)(z-1+i)=(z-1)^{2}-i^{2}\]
\[=z^{2}-2z+1+1\]
\[=z^{2}-2z+2\]
Why: Treat \((z-1)\) as one block \(A\): \((A-i)(A+i)=A^{2}-i^{2}\).

Check: P(2)
\[-48+48+168-192+96=72\]
Why: The condition holds.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (page 297) prints this answer under the label 7, as \(x=-3z^{4}+6z^{3}+42z^{2}-96z+96\). It is the answer to Question 8, and it should read \(P(z)=\) rather than \(x=\). The polynomial itself is correct.
